atoms.b: The British Parliament is in charge of passing laws and ((debating)) existing ones, making it the ((legislative)) branch of political institutions. It also challenges the government's decisions.
The government is responsible for carrying out ((laws)) and therefore represents the ((++executive)) branch.
The system of courts ((interprets)) laws and makes sure the government does not act against the law. It embodies the ((judicial)) branch and operates largely independently.

atoms.b: Parliament is bicameral, meaning it consists of two ((chambers)). The House of Lords forms the ((upper)) chamber and the House of Commons the ((lower)) chamber.

All seats in the House of Lords used to be inherited, but nowadays most members are ((appointed)) for life by the ((monarch)) upon advice from the prime minister. Members of the House of Lords are called peers. Most peers are senior politicians, while some are ((bishops)) of the Church of England.
Members of the House of Commons are called Members of ((Parliament)), or MPs. Each of the 650 MPs is ((voted)) into Parliament by British ((citizens)) aged 18 or older.

The UK is split into 650 electoral districts called constituencies. One constituency corresponds to one seat in the House of ((Commons)). During general elections every five years, residents of a constituency ((vote)) for their preferred candidate to become an MP and represent them in ((Parliament)). Most MP candidates join a political party in order to financially fund their ((campaign)).
The party winning the most ((seats)) in the House of Commons becomes the ((leading_party)). Their party leader, who is decided by a vote within the party, becomes ((prime_minister)).
